title: Pitot-static system
object: Pitot-static system of a four-seat high-wing light aircraft: the heated pitot head under the left wing with its ram hole, drain hole, water dam and heater; the two flush static ports on the tail cone, cross-connected; the lines, the drain traps and the alternate static valve; and the airspeed indicator, the altimeter and the vertical speed indicator, each in section and from the front with half its dial broken away to show the capsule, rocking shaft, sector, pinion and hairspring
idea: Three instruments read two pressures: total minus static is airspeed, static alone is height, and static against a deliberately leaky copy of itself is climb rate
summary: The pitot head stops the air, so its line holds total pressure, static plus about 1.97 kPa at 110 kt; the airspeed indicator's capsule feels only that difference and reads it on the sea-level law, so at 6500 ft the same 110 kt is 121 kt true. The altimeter's evacuated capsules swell as static pressure falls and its dial is the standard atmosphere's pressure-height law, set to the day's pressure with the Kollsman knob, about 27 ft a hectopascal. The VSI's case leaks to static through a Ø0.25 mm capillary, a first-order lag with τ = 8μLV/πr⁴p of 5.5 s at sea level, so a steady climb holds a steady Δp = ρgwτ. Block the ram hole and the open drain lets the pitot side fall to static: the ASI reads zero. Block the drain too and the trapped air turns the ASI into an altimeter, reading high in a climb. Ice the static ports and the altimeter freezes, the VSI sinks to zero and the ASI reads high in a descent; the alternate source brings them back from the cabin, a little low in pressure, so they read about 4 kt and 50 ft high.
usedFor: Pilot training: what each instrument senses, why IAS and TAS part with height, and the classic pitot and static blockages and their symptoms
Engineering courses: the standard atmosphere, impact pressure and compressible CAS, aneroid altimetry, a laminar capillary as an RC time constant, orifice flow
A software-concept explainer: a derivative computed by comparing a signal with a lagged copy of itself (the VSI is a high-pass filter), and a sensor that fails silent or fails plausible
